The armoury

Grave Wounds: each era's common weapons and armour, with the game's figures. Pick an era and print it.

Loaded at the breech with a metal or linen cartridge: the Sharps and Spencer carbines of the Civil War cavalry, and the Springfield of 1866 that the frontier infantry got in 1867 (a rifle-musket converted to a breech-loader, .50 calibre). No wound count sets it apart from the rifle-musket's: it rolls on the same tables, and fires faster.

Rolls on the Peninsular War table, which records where 97 bayonet wounds fell (thighs most, then arms and hands, then chest). Medieval (c.1180-1500)

13 weapons and 11 armour kits: what its careers start with and its price list sells. The war itself: The Medieval Wars

Weapons

WeaponUseStrikesRateHandsAgainst armourClose
Sword (arming sword)Reach 1cut 70%, pierce 30%-One--
Baseline weapon; the Visby tables are applied unchanged.
Halberd (axe blade, spike and hook)Reach 2cut 55%, pierce 35%, crush 10%-Twobeats 1 pierce step-
The Swiss weapon of the 15th century, 5-8 feet long (Winkler after Elgger): an axe blade to cut, a spike to thrust and a hook to drag a horseman down; the halberdiers were the least armoured men in the Swiss line. The spike ignores a step of armour against pierce (a design estimate). On the Dornach evidence it rolls on the cuts, which Cooper finds fit sword or halberd and cannot tell apart.
Bow (war arrows)Range 15 / 40 / 90 hexes (to 180 m)pierce 95%, cut 5%-Two--
Its own table is the US Army's 1865-71 arrow-wound reports (Plains and Apache bows, iron and flint heads). At Visby, 126 arrow and crossbow-bolt wounds fell much like the blade wounds, mostly on the lower body, so on the Visby tables it uses their weights unchanged. Arrows are pierce wounds, not gunfire: bleeding, deep tracks and infection; a barbed head left inside causes trouble for months.
Longbow (English war bow, bodkin and broadhead arrows)Range 20 / 60 / 125 hexes (to 250 m)pierce 95%, cut 5%-Twobeats 1 pierce step (mail, padded, hardened leather, jack only)-
Heavy war bow of the Hundred Years' War and the Wars of the Roses. Arrows mostly left soft-tissue wounds, so bone evidence under-counts them; at Towton a few head wounds are arrowheads. Heavy arrows punch through bare mail and jacks (ignores 1 step vs pierce, there only): mail alone let arrows through to a lethal depth at almost every shot (Jones, J. Medieval Military History XVIII, 2020). Plate, a coat of plates and mail over padding get their full steps: a longbow arrow carries about 70-83 J (McEwen) and 100 J sinks only 9 mm into medium-carbon steel, so "the plate protected the wearer" (Williams, Wallace Collection); mail over a gambeson "greatly reduce[s], but not eliminate[s]" the risk (Jones).
Handgun (early arquebus, c.1450-1520)Range 12 / 25 / 50 hexes (to 100 m)ballistic 100%1 a minuteTwoas rifleMusket butt, Dagger
The Swiss and Landsknecht handgun of about 1500 (Büchse, Hakenbüchse), fired with a match; the Swiss reckoned its reach at 150-200 paces (Winkler after Elgger), and it was less accurate than the later musket, so its range bands are shorter (a design estimate). A Willisau muster of 1490 had 50 guns to 400 pikes and halberds. It is offered on the Dornach tables: on the skull table it rolls on the five gunshot wounds, on the gameplay table as the rest of its weights.
Crossbow (bolts)Range 15 / 50 / 100 hexes (to 200 m)pierce 100%3 a minuteTwobeats 1 pierce step (mail, padded, hardened leather, jack only)Dagger
Visby's arrow and bolt wounds are counted together (126), mostly on the lower body; the Visby weights are used with a small head bias for aimed shots at the face and helmet. Heavy bolts punch through bare mail and cloth (ignores 1 step vs pierce, there only): as the longbow (Jones 2020). Not plate: quality armour was sold as "proof against the crossbow", and a 90 lb crossbow's bolt carries about 192 J (Williams, after McEwen).
Spear / lanceReach 2pierce 90%, cut 10%-One--
Thrusting weapon aimed at the centre mass and face over the shield rim.
Bill (English bill, hooked polearm)Reach 2cut 60%, pierce 30%, crush 10%-Twobeats 1 pierce step-
The common infantry polearm of the Wars of the Roses: a cleaving blade with a hook and spike on a long haft. On the Towton evidence table it rolls on the blade wounds. Its top spike thrusts as the halberd's does and ignores a step of armour against pierce (the step a design estimate, as the halberd's): a bill of c.1471 has a 10.5-inch top spike and a shorter back spike (Fordham, Medieval London objects), and the Mary Rose bills (1545) a top spike (Mary Rose Trust). The hook, to pull a man down, is not modelled.
Pike (long infantry pike, 1450s-1700)Reach 3pierce 95%, crush 5%-Two--
The pike of the pike-and-shot armies, 15-18 feet (4.5-5.5 m) long, couched or levelled at chest and face height; no count of pike wounds was found, so it rolls on the Visby melee table as a spear, with no shield (pikemen carried none) and more thrusts to the face and chest. Offered on the tables of its era (a table's era_melee).
Axe (hand or long-hafted)Reach 1cut 85%, crush 15%-Onebeats 1 cut step-
Visby work describes axes taking the legs out; leg bias reflects that. Heavy cuts bite through mail (ignores 1 step vs cut).
Dagger / knifeReach 1pierce 70%, cut 30%-One--
Grappling and finishing weapon. On medieval tables it seeks gaps at neck, face and armpit; elsewhere it uses the forensic knife-assault table as recorded.
Poleaxe (axe, hammer and spike)Reach 1crush 45%, pierce 35%, cut 20%-Twobeats 1 crush step; beats 1 pierce step-
The man-at-arms' weapon against plate: hammer and spike to crack or pierce armour (ignores 1 step vs crush and pierce: design estimate). On the Towton evidence table it rolls on the blunt-force wounds, which were mostly to the head and face.
Clubbed musket (butt stroke)Reach 1crush 100%-Two--
Swung like a club when there was no time to reload or no bayonet. Revolutionary War pensioners lost eyes and had skulls broken by it. Rolls on the Visby melee table with no shield; head bias is a design estimate.
